en: The Sūtra on Time and Non-Time Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in the Kalandaka Feeding Ground near Rājagṛha. At that time,
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall explain to you what is the proper time and what is not the proper time."
"Reflect upon this well!
The bhikṣus said, "So be it."
“World-Honored One,
we shall receive your instruction and listen.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In this regard, what constitutes the proper time and what constitutes the improper time?
A bhikṣu should know: "
During the eight months of winter, from the sixteenth to the thirtieth day, seven *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while five and a half *pada* constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the ninth month, eight *pada* constitute the proper time, while six *pada* and eight *aṅgula* constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the ninth month, nine *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while seven *pada* and six fingers constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the tenth month, ten *pada* constitute the proper time, while eight *pada* and three fingers constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the tenth month, eleven *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while nine *pada* and three finger-breadths constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, twelve *pada* constitute the proper time, while ten *pada* and six finger-breadths constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the eleventh month, eleven *pada* and a half constitute the proper time (*kāla*); ten *pada* and one finger-breadth constitutes the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, eleven *pada* constitute the proper time; nine *pada* and four finger-breadths constitute the improper time.

From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, during the spring equinox, ten *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while eight *pada* minus one finger-breadth constitutes the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the first month, nine and a half *pada* constitute the proper time, while seven *pada* minus three finger-breadths constitutes the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the first month, nine *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while six *pada* minus three fingers constitutes the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the second month, eight *pada* constitute the proper time, while five *pada* constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the second month, seven *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*); four *pada* minus three finger-breadths constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the third month, six *pada* constitute the proper time; three *pada* minus four finger-breadths constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the third month, five *pāda* constitute the proper time (*kāla*); three *pāda* minus six fingers constitutes the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the fourth month, four *pāda* constitute the proper time; two *pāda* minus one finger constitutes the improper time.

During the four months of summer, from the sixteenth to the thirtieth day, three quarters of the day constitute the proper time (*kāla*); two quarters minus four finger-breadths constitute the improper time (*vikāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, two quarters constitute the proper time; three quarters minus [four finger-breadths] constitute the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the fifth month, two and a half quarters constitute the proper time (*kāla*); slightly less than one quarter is the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the sixth month, four quarters constitute the proper time; slightly less than two quarters—by two finger-breadths—is the improper time.
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the sixth month, four and a half *pādas* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), and two and a half *pādas* constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the seventh month, five *pādas* constitute the proper time, and slightly less than three *pādas* constitute the improper time.

From the sixteenth to the thirtieth day of the seventh month, five quarters and a half of a *pada* constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while less than three quarters of a *pada* constitutes the improper time (*akāla*).
From the first to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, six quarters of a *pada* constitute the proper time, while less than four quarters of a *pada* constitutes the improper time.

From the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day of the eighth month, six and a half quarters constitute the proper time (*kāla*), while four and a half quarters less than that constitute the improper time (*akāla*).
"Thus it is, O bhikṣus!"

I have already explained the twelve months as being either the proper time or the improper time for those things which ought to be performed by the śrāvakas; this was spoken out of compassion and for their benefit.
What I was to do is now complete; you all should now proceed.
If you are under a tree, in an empty place, or sitting in the open air, contemplate with mindfulness. O bhikṣus!
Do not be negligent, lest you later feel regret.
"This is my instruction.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced; they encouraged one another to receive and uphold it.
"Because of the cause and condition of contempt, one falls into the evil realms at the end of life;
because of the cause and condition of practicing virtue, one is reborn in heaven in this life.
By virtue of cultivating wholesome karma through these conditions, one leaves evil behind and attains liberation."
"Failing to contemplate causes and conditions, one enters the evil realms when the body perishes.
The foreign Dharma Master Yìluóyán held the manuscript in the Hu language in his hand and translated it orally himself.
A monk from Liangzhou finished transcribing this within the city of Yutian.
Clad in coarse cloth yet harboring jade within; possessing profound wisdom while appearing as a fool;
outwardly like a commoner, yet inwardly cherishing a bright pearl.
For ten trillion *kalpas*, one is of the same essence as the Way.
From the *Buddhabhāṣita-kāla-akāla-sūtra*.
